script.opening: (Tearful, speaks quickly.) "Thanks for seeing me. My hair is falling out — properly, handfuls of it in the shower, it's all over my pillow, and it just looks thinner everywhere. I'm 28, I'm terrified I'm going bald. I've been crying about it, I don't want to go out. Is something seriously wrong with me? Please, I just need it to stop — can you give me something for it?"

facts.text: About three months of heavy shedding: "handfuls in the shower, hair all over my pillow and my jumper." It is thinner all over, not in patches. If asked: "No bald spots — it's just everywhere." Ponytail feels much thinner.
If asked: scalp feels normal — no itch, soreness, redness, scaling or flaking. No broken-off hairs she has noticed. Nails fine. Happy to show her parting and hairline on the camera if asked.

Only if asked about the months before: "Loads, actually. We moved house — it was a nightmare — then I had a flu-type thing and was in bed for a week with a temperature. And I went on a really strict diet to lose weight." All of that was about three to four months ago.
"I'm vegetarian anyway, and I cut right down on everything for a couple of months — mostly salads and soup." Lost about half a stone on the diet, on purpose. Eating normally again now.

If asked: "They're really heavy. I've always had heavy ones" — 7 days, flooding through a super tampon and pad on the heaviest days, regular cycle. Not pregnant — she and her partner use condoms; last period 2 weeks ago. Did not know periods could affect hair.

"I'm exhausted, but I thought that was the stress." If asked: no palpitations, no heat or cold intolerance, no weight change apart from the diet, bowels normal. No rashes, joint pains or mouth ulcers.
No regular medicines, no supplements, no contraceptive pill. No allergies. No previous hair or skin problems. Has not changed hair products; does not dye or tie it tightly.
If asked: "Mum's hair is fine. My nan went a bit thin on top when she was old." No family thyroid disease she knows of.
Primary school teacher, lives with her partner. Doesn't smoke, drinks a glass of wine at weekends. Has stopped going out with friends: "I don't want anyone to see it."
Only if asked kindly: "I get through work. But evenings I just feel low and check my hair constantly." Sleep is poor. No thoughts of self-harm — "No, nothing like that."

Anxious, tearful at the start; calms if the doctor takes her seriously. Volunteer the shedding and the distress; hold back the house move, illness, diet and heavy periods until asked. If told "it'll grow back, don't worry" without explanation, become more upset: "You're not the one losing it." If given a clear reason and a timeline, ask "So it'll grow back? Months though… that's hard" and then relax.

ice.ideas: "I think I'm going bald — or something is really wrong with me inside."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — "It's silly, but it's me — it's how I feel like myself." Her hair is central to how she sees herself; she has stopped going out, feels low in the evenings and is quietly scared it means a serious illness. She only says this if the doctor asks what it means to her.
ice.expectations: "Something to make it stop. And to know it's not something awful."

cues: "Sorry, I've been crying about it all week." — said early; she opens up about mood if this is picked up.
"It's just everywhere, not patches." — answers the pattern question if asked.
"I've stopped going out." — only expands on the identity and low mood if invited.

checkpoints.text: Recognises DIFFUSE shedding ~3 months after a trigger as likely TELOGEN EFFLUVIUM (reactive, usually reversible) and distinguishes it from androgenetic/patterned thinning, alopecia areata (discrete patches) and scarring alopecia (which needs prompt dermatology referral)
Identifies the TRIGGER(S) (stressful move, flu-like illness, crash diet) and explains the delayed-shed mechanism (shedding starts about 2–6 months after the trigger, PCDS 2024)

Checks reversible CONTRIBUTORS with appropriate tests: FERRITIN/iron studies (heavy periods + vegetarian/crash diet), THYROID function (TFTs), and considers nutrition, recent drugs and pregnancy — and treats deficiencies found

Gives REASONED reassurance (not a brush-off): explains telogen effluvium recovers once the trigger resolves and contributors are corrected, with an HONEST timeline (regrowth over months), rather than "don’t worry, it’ll grow back"

Screens for and addresses MOOD/psychological impact and knows when to refer (scarring alopecia, diagnostic uncertainty, patterned loss wanting treatment, no recovery) — avoiding both over-investigation and dismissal
ACKNOWLEDGES what the hair means to her — identity, self-esteem, the distress and social withdrawal — and validates it, rather than minimising; treats reassurance as a skilled, empathic task
Engages her in the plan and the timeline so she feels heard and hopeful, and supports the emotional impact and any low mood

Safety-nets and follows up: the ferritin/TFT results and contributor treatment, the expected regrowth timeline and what would prompt review/referral (patchy/scarring loss, no recovery), mood support, and a follow-up — structured work-up + reassurance + emotional validation

worked.txt: "Before anything medical — I can see how much this is upsetting you, and I want to say your hair matters and this is NOT vain or silly. Crying about it, not wanting to go out — that’s a real and understandable response. So I’m going to take it seriously and we’ll work it out together."

"The good news, and I mean it with reasons not just to comfort you: hair that thins ALL over like this, a few months after a stressful or unwell patch, is almost always something called telogen effluvium. A shock to the system — your illness, the move, the crash diet — tips lots of hairs into their resting-then-shedding phase a couple of months later. It looks alarming, but it’s reactive and it RECOVERS. You’re not going bald."

"To help it bounce back fastest, let’s check a couple of things that can keep it shedding — your iron levels, especially with heavy periods and being vegetarian and the diet, and your thyroid. If your iron’s low, topping it up genuinely helps the hair as well as your energy."

"I’ll be straight about timing so you’re not disheartened: the shedding usually settles within about six to nine months of starting, and the regrowth then comes through gradually over the months after that — you might even see little new short hairs at your hairline. It’s not instant, but it does come back."

"I’d like to have a proper look at your scalp in person — I can’t examine it properly on video, so let’s book you in at the surgery when you come for the blood test — just to be sure it’s this even shedding and not a patchy type or anything affecting the scalp itself, which we’d handle differently. From what you describe, it sounds like the reversible kind."

"And how are you in yourself with all this — mood-wise? … This kind of thing can really get you down, and that’s worth supporting too. So: I’ll check your iron and thyroid, we’ll treat anything low, and I’ll see you to follow the regrowth. If it ever became patchy, or the scalp looked scarred, or it’s not recovering, we’d look again — but I’m expecting your hair back. You’re not losing it for good."

f.learning: Diffuse hair shedding all over (not a discrete patch) ~2–6 months after a trigger (PCDS Hair Loss Pathway 2024) — illness/fever, childbirth, surgery, crash diet, severe stress, certain drugs — is the classic picture of TELOGEN EFFLUVIUM, a reactive, usually self-limiting and reversible shed. Identify the trigger and check reversible CONTRIBUTORS (ferritin/iron — here heavy periods + vegetarian/crash diet; TFTs; nutrition; drugs; pregnancy), distinguish it from androgenetic/patterned thinning, alopecia areata (discrete patches) and scarring alopecia (prompt dermatology), and treat deficiencies. The reassurance (recovery) is true and central — but delivered as a brush-off ("it’ll grow back") it dismisses real distress; give REASONED reassurance with an honest regrowth timeline (months). The examinable hidden agenda is that the consultation is as much about IDENTITY and self-esteem as the scalp: at 28 her hair is central to how she sees herself, the shedding has caused distress, social withdrawal and possibly low mood. Acknowledge what the hair MEANS to her, validate it, support mood, and combine structured work-up + reassurance + emotional validation.

knowledge.guideline: PCDS Hair Loss Pathway (Nov 2024) · BAD patient information: telogen effluvium (Oct 2025) · BSG iron deficiency anaemia guideline 2021 · NICE NG88 · NICE NG145 · NICE NG222
knowledge.summary: Diffuse shedding a few months after a trigger is telogen effluvium: reactive and reversible. Check FBC, ferritin and TFTs, look for patterned, patchy or scarring loss, and treat the distress as part of the problem.

points.t: Diffuse, non-scarring shedding all over the scalp, starting 2–6 months after a trigger and usually settling by 6–9 months (PCDS Hair Loss Pathway 2024). Triggers include febrile illness, childbirth, surgery, crash dieting, severe stress and some drugs. A gentle hair-pull test is often positive.

PCDS advises FBC, ferritin and thyroid function for diffuse hair loss. Ferritin is the single most useful marker of iron deficiency (BSG 2021). Heavy periods warrant an FBC in their own right (NICE NG88).
Replace iron if deficient and look for the cause — here heavy periods and a restricted diet. Oral iron dose per BNF. Manage abnormal thyroid function per NICE NG145.

Androgenetic (female pattern) loss: widening central parting, frontal hairline kept. Alopecia areata: discrete smooth patches with exclamation-mark hairs. Scarring alopecia: loss of follicle openings, redness, scale or pain — refer urgently to dermatology to prevent permanent loss (PCDS 2024).
Hair loss commonly causes low mood, anxiety and social withdrawal. Ask about mood and, where low, assess and support per NICE NG222 (depression in adults).
Shedding eases over the following months and regrowth is gradual; short new hairs at the hairline are a good sign. Topical minoxidil is not a routine treatment for telogen effluvium.

dg.d: Open question; acknowledged the distress in the booking note and let her describe the shedding fully.
Work as a teacher, the house move, strict dieting, vegetarian diet, and social withdrawal.
Video look at the scalp with a face-to-face offer; FBC, ferritin and TFTs; asked about pregnancy and drugs.
Telogen effluvium versus female pattern loss, alopecia areata, scarring alopecia, iron deficiency and thyroid disease.
Screened for scarring alopecia (itch, pain, redness, scale) and asked directly about low mood and risk.
Named telogen effluvium with the trigger and mechanism, and an honest recovery timeline.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Tests for contributors, iron replacement if low (dose per BNF), attention to heavy periods, mood support; no minoxidil for telogen effluvium.
Heavy menstrual bleeding and restricted diet as the likely cause of iron deficiency; low mood addressed.
Named triggers for review (patches, scalp changes, no improvement at 6 months, worsening mood) and booked follow-up with results.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options

Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

Idea (going bald, something serious); concern (identity, social withdrawal, low evenings); expectation (make it stop).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — "It's silly, but it's me — it's how I feel like myself." Her hair is central to how she sees herself; she has stopped going out, feels low in the evenings and is quietly scared it means a serious illness. She only says this if the doctor asks what it means to her — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Carys, I’m Dr Lee. I can see from your note you’re really worried about your hair. Tell me what’s been happening, from the start.
model.why: Open question; acknowledges the distress in the booking note

model.text: It’s coming out in handfuls in the shower, it’s all over my pillow, and it just looks thinner everywhere. I’m 28 — I’m terrified I’m going bald. I just need it to stop.
That sounds frightening, and I can hear how upset you are. I want to understand exactly what’s going on, have a look, and then agree a plan with you. Is that okay?
model.why: Acknowledges emotion and sets an agenda

model.text: Yes. Sorry, I’ve been crying about it all week.
No need to apologise at all. When did you first notice it, and is it thinning all over, or are there any bald patches?
model.why: Pattern and timing — diffuse versus patchy

model.text: About three months ago. It’s everywhere, not patches.
Think back to a few months before that — anything big happen? Illness, stress, changes in eating?
model.why: Looks for the trigger 2–6 months earlier

model.text: Loads, actually. We moved house, which was a nightmare, then I had a flu-type thing and was in bed for a week. And I did a really strict diet to lose weight.
That’s really helpful. What sort of diet — and are you vegetarian?
model.why: Nutritional contributors to iron deficiency

model.text: I’m vegetarian anyway, and I cut right down on everything for a couple of months.
And your periods — are they heavy at all? Flooding, or needing to change very often?
model.why: Iron loss from heavy menstrual bleeding

model.text: They’re really heavy. I’ve always had heavy ones.
Is there any chance you could be pregnant, and are you taking any medicines, supplements or anything new?
model.why: Pregnancy and drug causes

model.text: No, not pregnant. No medicines.
Any feeling tired, cold or hot all the time, palpitations, or weight change you didn’t intend?
model.why: Thyroid and anaemia screen

model.text: I’m exhausted, but I thought that was the stress.
Does your scalp itch, burn or feel sore anywhere, or have you seen redness or scaly areas?
model.why: Screens for scarring alopecia

model.text: No, the scalp feels normal.
You said you’ve been crying all week. What does losing your hair mean for you?
model.why: Explores meaning and identity rather than just the symptom

model.text: It’s silly, but it’s me — it’s how I feel like myself. I’ve stopped going out. I keep thinking something serious is wrong with me.
It isn’t silly at all. How has your mood been generally — are you still enjoying things, sleeping, managing at work?
model.why: Mood screen prompted by social withdrawal

model.text: I get through work. But evenings I just feel low and check my hair constantly.
Thank you for telling me that. What were you hoping we could do today?
model.why: Elicits expectations

model.text: Something to make it stop. And to know it’s not something awful.

Could you show me the top of your head and your parting on the camera? … Thank you. That looks like even thinning, the hairline is intact, and I can’t see patches or any redness. I’d still like to see you in person to look more closely.
model.why: Examination adapted to video, with a face-to-face offer

model.text: From everything you’ve told me, this sounds very much like telogen effluvium. A shock to the body — your illness, the move, the strict diet — makes lots of hairs switch into their resting phase together, and a couple of months later they all fall out at once. It’s alarming, but it’s reactive and it recovers. You are not going bald.
model.why: Names the diagnosis with a reasoned mechanism

model.text: So it’ll grow back?

Yes. I’ll be honest about timing: the shedding usually eases over the next few months, and regrowth is gradual, so it takes a while to see the thickness return. Look for short new hairs at the front — that’s a good sign.
model.why: Honest timeline rather than a brush-off

model.text: Months though… that’s hard.

It is, and I won’t pretend otherwise. What I can do is make sure nothing is keeping it going. With heavy periods, being vegetarian and that diet, you may be low in iron — and the tiredness fits. So I’d like a blood count, iron stores and thyroid test.
model.why: Targets reversible contributors: ferritin, FBC, TFTs

model.text: If your iron is low, we’ll treat it, and look at the heavy periods too — there are good treatments for those. What do you think?
model.why: Shares the plan and links it to her other symptoms

model.text: Yes. I didn’t know periods could do this.
And the low evenings — would it help to talk more about that? There’s support available, and I’d like to see how you are when we go through the results.
model.why: Offers mood support and follow-up

model.text: Maybe. It helps just saying it out loud.

If you see a smooth bald patch, redness, scaling or soreness on the scalp, or it’s still shedding heavily in six months, tell me — those need a different approach. And if your mood gets worse or you have any thoughts of harming yourself, contact us the same day.
model.why: Specific safety-net for scarring or patchy loss and mood

model.text: Okay.
So what will you tell a friend tonight about what’s happening?
model.why: Teach-back

model.text: That it’s a shed after a rough few months, it grows back, and I’m getting my iron and thyroid checked.
Exactly right. Book the blood test this week and a face-to-face with me in two weeks. Anything else before we finish?
model.why: Confirms follow-up and shares the floor

model.text: No. Thank you — I feel less mad.

social.t: Hair is closely tied to self-image; avoiding social events and constant checking are signs of real distress and possible low mood.
A vegetarian diet plus a recent crash diet raises iron and nutritional risk — explore without judgement and consider dietitian input if restriction continues.

legal.t: She is managing at work; no fit note is needed. If low mood worsens and affects work, a fit note can be considered.

professional.t: A video look at the scalp is useful but limited; offering a face-to-face examination to exclude scarring or patchy loss reflects GMC Good Medical Practice (2024).
Explain why supplements beyond correcting a proven deficiency, and minoxidil, are not indicated for telogen effluvium.

community.t: British Association of Dermatologists patient information leaflet on telogen effluvium; Alopecia UK for peer support; NHS Talking Therapies self-referral if mood is low.

redFlags: Scalp redness, scale, pain, burning or loss of follicle openings — possible scarring alopecia, urgent dermatology
Symptoms of anaemia or thyroid disease; heavy menstrual bleeding
Low mood, withdrawal, any thoughts of self-harm
psychosocial: Teacher, managing at work but withdrawing socially
Recent stressful house move and strict dieting
What her hair means to her identity
ice: Idea: “I’m going bald — something is seriously wrong.”
Concern: losing part of herself; avoiding friends; feeling low

playbook.diagnosis: “This is telogen effluvium — a delayed shed after a shock to the system. It looks alarming, but it’s reactive and it recovers once the trigger has passed and anything like low iron is corrected.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of your hairs as a crowd that normally leaves a few at a time. A big shock — illness, stress, dieting — makes lots of them head for the exit together a couple of months later. Once the crowd has left, new ones come back in, but it takes months.”

management.reflectIce: “You told me your hair is how you feel like yourself — that’s exactly why I want to find and fix anything slowing its recovery.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the withdrawal and low evenings, offer support, and agree a realistic timeline so she isn’t checking daily for change.
sharedPlan: FBC, ferritin, TFTs; face-to-face scalp examination
Treat iron deficiency (dose per BNF) and address heavy periods
Mood support and review with results
safetyNet: Patches, scalp redness or soreness, or no improvement by 6 months — review and consider dermatology
Worsening mood or thoughts of self-harm — contact the same day

pitfalls.intro: Candidates usually know telogen effluvium. The station is failed on how the reassurance is delivered, on missing the iron picture, and on ignoring what the hair loss is doing to her.

items.fail: “It’ll grow back, don’t worry” within the first three minutes.
items.why: Reassurance before understanding reads as dismissal: “Does not take the patient’s concerns seriously.”
items.fix: Hear the history and the meaning first, then explain the mechanism so the reassurance is earned.

items.fail: No question about periods or diet.
items.why: Heavy periods, a vegetarian diet and crash dieting are the treatable contributors; missing them is incomplete data gathering.
items.fix: Ask directly and check FBC, ferritin and TFTs, as PCDS advises for diffuse hair loss.

items.fail: Offering minoxidil or supplements as the fix.
items.why: Neither treats telogen effluvium; it signals a management plan not based on the diagnosis.
items.fix: Treat proven deficiencies and give an honest recovery timeline.

items.fail: Not looking at the scalp or asking about scalp symptoms.
items.why: Scarring alopecia needs urgent referral and can be missed without asking about pain, redness or scale.
items.fix: Look on camera, ask the scalp questions, and offer a face-to-face examination.

items.fail: Ignoring “I’ve stopped going out” and the tears.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to cues.” The social withdrawal is the emotional core of the case.
items.fix: “You said you’ve stopped going out — how has your mood been?”

items.fail: Closing without saying when to come back or what would change the plan.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and no follow-up are standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Name patches, scalp changes, no improvement by six months and worsening mood; book the results review.

timeMap.d: She arrives tearful. Acknowledge it before the history — “you’ve been crying all week” is your cue.
Diffuse or patchy; timing; trigger 2–6 months earlier (illness, move, diet); periods, diet, pregnancy, drugs, thyroid symptoms; scalp symptoms.
What her hair means to her, the social withdrawal, and a direct mood question.
Scalp on camera, face-to-face offer. Telogen effluvium with mechanism and honest timeline. FBC, ferritin, TFTs; heavy periods.
Patches, scalp changes, no recovery, worsening mood. Teach-back. Results and review in two weeks.

SCA_MODELS.text: So it’ll grow back?

Yes. I’ll be honest about timing: the shedding usually eases over the next few months, and regrowth is gradual, so it takes a while to see the thickness return. Look for short new hairs at the front — that’s a good sign.
SCA_MODELS.why: Honest timeline rather than a brush-off

SCA_MODELS.text: Months though… that’s hard.

It is, and I won’t pretend otherwise. What I can do is make sure nothing is keeping it going. With heavy periods, being vegetarian and that diet, you may be low in iron — and the tiredness fits. So I’d like a blood count, iron stores and thyroid test.
SCA_MODELS.why: Targets reversible contributors: ferritin, FBC, TFTs

SCA_MODELS.text: If your iron is low, we’ll treat it, and look at the heavy periods too — there are good treatments for those. What do you think?
SCA_MODELS.why: Shares the plan and links it to her other symptoms

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes. I didn’t know periods could do this.
And the low evenings — would it help to talk more about that? There’s support available, and I’d like to see how you are when we go through the results.
SCA_MODELS.why: Offers mood support and follow-up

SCA_MODELS.text: Maybe. It helps just saying it out loud.

If you see a smooth bald patch, redness, scaling or soreness on the scalp, or it’s still shedding heavily in six months, tell me — those need a different approach. And if your mood gets worse or you have any thoughts of harming yourself, contact us the same day.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety-net for scarring or patchy loss and mood

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay.
So what will you tell a friend tonight about what’s happening?
SCA_MODELS.why: Teach-back

SCA_MODELS.text: That it’s a shed after a rough few months, it grows back, and I’m getting my iron and thyroid checked.
Exactly right. Book the blood test this week and a face-to-face with me in two weeks. Anything else before we finish?
SCA_MODELS.why: Confirms follow-up and shares the floor

SCA_MODELS.text: No. Thank you — I feel less mad.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: PCDS Hair Loss Pathway (Nov 2024) · BAD patient information: telogen effluvium (Oct 2025) · BSG iron deficiency anaemia guideline 2021 · NICE NG88 · NICE NG145 · NICE NG222
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Diffuse shedding a few months after a trigger is telogen effluvium: reactive and reversible. Check FBC, ferritin and TFTs, look for patterned, patchy or scarring loss, and treat the distress as part of the problem.

points.t: Diffuse, non-scarring shedding all over the scalp, starting 2–6 months after a trigger and usually settling by 6–9 months (PCDS Hair Loss Pathway 2024). Triggers include febrile illness, childbirth, surgery, crash dieting, severe stress and some drugs. A gentle hair-pull test is often positive.

PCDS advises FBC, ferritin and thyroid function for diffuse hair loss. Ferritin is the single most useful marker of iron deficiency (BSG 2021). Heavy periods warrant an FBC in their own right (NICE NG88).
Replace iron if deficient and look for the cause — here heavy periods and a restricted diet. Oral iron dose per BNF. Manage abnormal thyroid function per NICE NG145.

Androgenetic (female pattern) loss: widening central parting, frontal hairline kept. Alopecia areata: discrete smooth patches with exclamation-mark hairs. Scarring alopecia: loss of follicle openings, redness, scale or pain — refer urgently to dermatology to prevent permanent loss (PCDS 2024).
Hair loss commonly causes low mood, anxiety and social withdrawal. Ask about mood and, where low, assess and support per NICE NG222 (depression in adults).
Shedding eases over the following months and regrowth is gradual; short new hairs at the hairline are a good sign. Topical minoxidil is not a routine treatment for telogen effluvium.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; acknowledged the distress in the booking note and let her describe the shedding fully.
Work as a teacher, the house move, strict dieting, vegetarian diet, and social withdrawal.
Picked up “crying all week” and “I’ve stopped going out”, and the tiredness, and explored each.
Idea (going bald, something serious); concern (identity, social withdrawal, low evenings); expectation (make it stop).
Video look at the scalp with a face-to-face offer; FBC, ferritin and TFTs; asked about pregnancy and drugs.
Telogen effluvium versus female pattern loss, alopecia areata, scarring alopecia, iron deficiency and thyroid disease.
Screened for scarring alopecia (itch, pain, redness, scale) and asked directly about low mood and risk.
Named telogen effluvium with the trigger and mechanism, and an honest recovery timeline.
Tests for contributors, iron replacement if low (dose per BNF), attention to heavy periods, mood support; no minoxidil for telogen effluvium.
Heavy menstrual bleeding and restricted diet as the likely cause of iron deficiency; low mood addressed.
Named triggers for review (patches, scalp changes, no improvement at 6 months, worsening mood) and booked follow-up with results.

social.t: Hair is closely tied to self-image; avoiding social events and constant checking are signs of real distress and possible low mood.
A vegetarian diet plus a recent crash diet raises iron and nutritional risk — explore without judgement and consider dietitian input if restriction continues.

legal.t: She is managing at work; no fit note is needed. If low mood worsens and affects work, a fit note can be considered.

professional.t: A video look at the scalp is useful but limited; offering a face-to-face examination to exclude scarring or patchy loss reflects GMC Good Medical Practice (2024).
Explain why supplements beyond correcting a proven deficiency, and minoxidil, are not indicated for telogen effluvium.

community.t: British Association of Dermatologists patient information leaflet on telogen effluvium; Alopecia UK for peer support; NHS Talking Therapies self-referral if mood is low.

redFlags: Scalp redness, scale, pain, burning or loss of follicle openings — possible scarring alopecia, urgent dermatology
Symptoms of anaemia or thyroid disease; heavy menstrual bleeding
Low mood, withdrawal, any thoughts of self-harm
psychosocial: Teacher, managing at work but withdrawing socially
Recent stressful house move and strict dieting
What her hair means to her identity
ice: Idea: “I’m going bald — something is seriously wrong.”
Concern: losing part of herself; avoiding friends; feeling low

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is telogen effluvium — a delayed shed after a shock to the system. It looks alarming, but it’s reactive and it recovers once the trigger has passed and anything like low iron is corrected.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of your hairs as a crowd that normally leaves a few at a time. A big shock — illness, stress, dieting — makes lots of them head for the exit together a couple of months later. Once the crowd has left, new ones come back in, but it takes months.”

management.reflectIce: “You told me your hair is how you feel like yourself — that’s exactly why I want to find and fix anything slowing its recovery.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the withdrawal and low evenings, offer support, and agree a realistic timeline so she isn’t checking daily for change.
sharedPlan: FBC, ferritin, TFTs; face-to-face scalp examination
Treat iron deficiency (dose per BNF) and address heavy periods
Mood support and review with results
safetyNet: Patches, scalp redness or soreness, or no improvement by 6 months — review and consider dermatology
Worsening mood or thoughts of self-harm — contact the same day

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: Candidates usually know telogen effluvium. The station is failed on how the reassurance is delivered, on missing the iron picture, and on ignoring what the hair loss is doing to her.

items.fail: “It’ll grow back, don’t worry” within the first three minutes.
items.why: Reassurance before understanding reads as dismissal: “Does not take the patient’s concerns seriously.”
items.fix: Hear the history and the meaning first, then explain the mechanism so the reassurance is earned.

items.fail: No question about periods or diet.
items.why: Heavy periods, a vegetarian diet and crash dieting are the treatable contributors; missing them is incomplete data gathering.
items.fix: Ask directly and check FBC, ferritin and TFTs, as PCDS advises for diffuse hair loss.

items.fail: Offering minoxidil or supplements as the fix.
items.why: Neither treats telogen effluvium; it signals a management plan not based on the diagnosis.
items.fix: Treat proven deficiencies and give an honest recovery timeline.

items.fail: Not looking at the scalp or asking about scalp symptoms.
items.why: Scarring alopecia needs urgent referral and can be missed without asking about pain, redness or scale.
items.fix: Look on camera, ask the scalp questions, and offer a face-to-face examination.

items.fail: Ignoring “I’ve stopped going out” and the tears.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to cues.” The social withdrawal is the emotional core of the case.
items.fix: “You said you’ve stopped going out — how has your mood been?”

items.fail: Closing without saying when to come back or what would change the plan.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and no follow-up are standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Name patches, scalp changes, no improvement by six months and worsening mood; book the results review.
